newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Japan PM seeks to boost Asian political profile.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM seeks to boost Asian political profile.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, fresh from his summit in Washington, arrives here on Monday on a visit aimed at broadening ties with Canberra and boosting Tokyo's political profile in the Asia-Pacific region.
Hashimoto, a former fiery trade minister who began his second term as prime minister in November, hopes to expand the focus of bilateral ties once centred mostly on economic issues.

"Previously, Japan's ties with Australia developed focusing on economic issues. Now we would like to strengthen political ties, including the relationship between our leaders," a Japanese diplomat said ahead of Hashimoto's visit.

As a symbol of that desire, Hashimoto is expected to propose annual Australia-Japan summits, a move that might appear more form than substance given that leaders of the two nations already meet on a fairly regular basis.

With no serious two-way feuds to distract them, Hashimoto and Prime Minister John Howard are likely to discuss a plethora of bilateral, regional and global issues such as U.S.-Japan ties, China, North Korea, and economic cooperation in forums such as the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) grouping.

Japanese officials said Hashimoto would reaffirm Tokyo's support for Australia's bid to join the Asia Europe Meeting (ASEM), which links Brunei, Malaysia, Indonesia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam, Japan, China and South Korea with the 15-member European Union.
He will also listen to Canberra's complaints about market access for its agricultural products, including rice.
"Certainly the prime minister and I and others will be raising the question of expanded and fairer rice market access," Australian deputy prime minister Tim Fischer said on Sunday.
Asked in a television interview if he expected success in that area, he said: "Bit by bit, yes."
Ever keen to present Japan as a real political player in the Asia-Pacific, Hashimoto will deliver a speech outlining his stance toward the region in Canberra on Monday.

Hashimoto made a stab at pitching a new view of Japan's role in Asia last January, capping a tour of five Southeast Asian nations by proposing tighter political ties with the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN).

"Hashimoto has always had his eye on Asia. It's not just Hashimoto, it's government policy to expand Japan's political role in the region," said John Neuffer, a political analyst at Mitsui Marine Research Institute in Tokyo.
"I don't think that the Japanese really know what they mean by saying that, but at least they give the impression they are not the same old political animal," he added.

Japan, however, remains deeply ambivalent over whether it should assume a higher-profile role in regional non-economic affairs, given constitutional limits on military action abroad and a traditional alliance on the U.S. security umbrella.
Many of Japan's Asian neighbours are equally wary about a bigger regional role for Tokyo.

"Japan is not a great power," one former Japanese official said recently. "A sense of 'power' must come from a nation's sense of history, political and culture. I think Japan has economic power, but in a political sense I don't think Japan could create much more influence in this region."
On Wednesday, Hashimoto flies to Wellington for talks with Prime Minister Jim Bolger and other members of his coalition government installed last December.
While in New Zealand, Hashimoto -- an experienced mountaineer -- will take a break from formal diplomacy with a "bush walk" outside Wellington.
